issues.legal_issue: Non-hereditary trustees may not be appointed while the public character of an institution or the existence of hereditary trustees is disputed unless those matters have first been determined through the prescribed adjudicative process.
material_facts: Villagers sought appointment of non-hereditary trustees for a temple under the statutory appointment provision.
The respondents objected that the institution was private and, alternatively, that they were hereditary trustees.
The authority appointed non-hereditary trustees after a summary inquiry that found the institution public but did not determine whether the respondents were hereditary trustees.
The authority later directed delivery of the institution and its property to the appointed trustees.
The High Court quashed the orders, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.
issues.conclusion: Where either relevant status is disputed, the authority must first determine the dispute in the prescribed adjudicative proceeding; the appointment and consequential possession orders made without that determination were without jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 27 and 41 of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, appointment under section 27 depends on the institution being public and there being no hereditary trustee. Section 41 provides for determination of disputes about those matters, and section 44 provides an appeal from that determination. The differing procedures, appeal rights, and absence of a provision making a section 27 decision provisional show that section 27 cannot be used to bypass a disputed determination under section 41. Section 68 cannot support delivery of possession on the basis of an invalid appointment. The Court relied on Ramakrishna Padhy v. Ramesh Chandra Das, Sri Sadasib Prakash Brahmachari v. State of Orissa, and Sri Jagannath Ramanuja Das v. State of Orissa.

predicates.trustee_appointment_proceeding: An authority is considering appointing non-hereditary trustees for a religious institution.
predicates.relevant_status_disputed: A person contests whether the institution is public or whether hereditary trustees exist.
predicates.no_prior_adjudicative_determination: The disputed status has not previously been determined through the proceeding that allows the parties to present evidence and challenge the determination.

issues.definition: When a trustee-appointment proceeding concerns a disputed institutional or trustee status that has not been adjudicated, the appointment lacks jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A proceeding determining disputed institutional status or hereditary trusteeship must provide a judicial and sufficiently elaborate inquiry rather than a summary inquiry.
material_facts: The respondents contested the institution's public character and claimed hereditary trusteeship.

The appointment authority conducted only a summary inquiry, in which the affected persons did not receive a full opportunity to present their case and evidence was not recorded in the manner required for an elaborate adjudication.
The statutory scheme provided a separate proceeding for determining the disputed status and an appeal from its determination.
issues.conclusion: A summary inquiry associated with trustee appointment is not a substitute for the judicial and elaborate inquiry required to determine the disputed status.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 provides for adjudication of disputes about whether an institution is public and whether a trustee is hereditary. Under section 44, decisions in that proceeding are appealable. Section 74 and Rule 43 require the civil-procedure and evidence rules to be followed as far as practicable in proceedings of the relevant adjudicative character. By contrast, an inquiry connected with section 27 is summary and does not provide the same opportunity to present the entire case. The Court relied on Ramakrishna Padhy v. Ramesh Chandra Das.

predicates.status_determination_proceeding: An authority is conducting a proceeding to determine the public character of an institution or the existence of hereditary trustees.
predicates.affected_persons_contest_relevant_status: People affected by the determination dispute the institution's character or the trustees' status.

issues.definition: When a proceeding determines a contested institutional or trustee status, the inquiry must be judicial and elaborate.

issues.legal_issue: An endowments authority may initiate an inquiry into specified status disputes on its own motion when the governing law does not prohibit that course.
material_facts: The appellants argued that a properly verified application with the required fee was necessary to determine disputes of the kind specified in the Act.
The respondents had also filed an application raising the disputed status, but no proceedings were taken on it.
The Court rejected the contention that an individual's application requirement, absent a specific prohibition, prevented the authority from initiating an inquiry on its own motion.
issues.conclusion: The authority may initiate an inquiry on its own motion into a dispute within the statutory inquiry power when there is no specific prohibition against doing so.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 empowers the Assistant Commissioner to inquire into and decide specified disputes. The requirement that a private individual make a verified application with the proper fee does not, in the absence of a specific prohibition, prevent the authority from acting on its own motion.

predicates.status_dispute_inquiry: A proceeding concerns a dispute about an institution's public character or a trustee's status.
predicates.authority_initiates_on_own_motion: The authority begins the inquiry without an application from a private person.
predicates.no_rule_prohibits_official_initiation: The governing rules contain no specific bar to the authority beginning that inquiry on its own motion.

issues.definition: If an authority begins a status-dispute inquiry on its own motion and no rule bars that course, it may conduct the inquiry.
